title: The sermon
hookLine: Catholics and Orthodox call it a homily; Protestants often a sermon

cards: A Sabbath day in Nazareth, his hometown. Jesus goes to the synagogue, as Luke says was his custom, and stands up to read.
He's handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, finds a place, and reads about good news to the poor and freedom for captives. Then Luke slows everything down.
"And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." Every eye in the room, waiting.
He begins with one sentence: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."

teach.h: READ, GIVE THE SENSE, HELP THEM.
teach.b: Catholics and Orthodox Christians usually call it a homily; Protestants often call it a sermon.
Both name the same moment: the scripture has been read, and now someone stands, or sits, to open it up. First, an old shape.

Long before Nazareth, in the book of Nehemiah, the people gather in Jerusalem by the water gate to hear the law read aloud, and the text says: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."
Read it, give the sense, help them understand. That's the job. Second, the words.
A homily, in Catholic and Orthodox use, stays close to the readings just heard; it's usually short, and it walks from the page to the table.

A sermon, in some Protestant churches, can range more widely, take one passage deep, and run longer; it's often the center of the service, as this block saw a few days ago. Same job, different weight.
Jesus told a crowd, "Take heed therefore how ye hear." Preaching isn't finished when the preacher sits down. It's finished when somebody carries something out the door.
Fourth, the one line. At Nazareth, Luke gives the heart of it in a single sentence. Homilies run longer than that.
But what stays, years later, can be one thing a preacher said: a phrase that landed, a story.
So a good way to hear any homily or sermon is to listen for the one line to keep.

how: At Catholic Mass and the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, a priest or deacon gives a homily on the readings just proclaimed; in Protestant services the sermon, often longer, is usually preached by the pastor and frequently stands at the center of worship.

s: a homily and a sermon are completely different things
both name the same moment: scripture read, then opened up. the words carry different weight in different churches.
at Nazareth, Luke gives the heart of Jesus's words in a single sentence
"This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."
in Nehemiah, the people heard the law read with no explanation
they "gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

games.q: you're in the synagogue at Nazareth. Jesus has read from Isaiah, closed the book and sat down. every eye is on him. what does he say?
o: a long explanation of the prophet's life.
"this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."
games.why: one sentence first. Luke puts the heart of it in a line, and the room's reaction fills the rest of the scene.

practice: Bring back a sermon or homily you've heard, recent or long ago; if none comes, use one of these past few lessons.
Ask what it was actually saying, squeeze it into one sentence short enough for a single breath, and say it quietly to yourself, twice. If you pray, hand that line to God and ask for help to live it.

wordCard.voice: Homily. What Catholics and Orthodox call the talk that opens up the readings just heard; Protestants often call it a sermon.

carryVoice: Your line: one line to keep. Years later, what stays is often a single sentence. Until tomorrow.
